title: Session KV resilience & on-prem routing deep dive - Lyra Labs
summary: Customer experiencing increased KV eviction and paging under sustained long-context chat sessions on their on-prem deployment. Symptoms include elevated tail latency during bursts, prefix hotspot churn when multiple users hit shared conversation templates, and degraded cache hit rate after rolling restarts. SE walked through telemetry, suggested prefetch threshold tuning, session windowing, and routing/affinity changes. Agreed next steps include running a controlled repro with load generator, sharing memory/profile dumps, and a follow-up canary test on a dedicated node pool.
action_items: Taylor: Share diagnostic runbook + telemetry query examples by 2026-11-15
Jordan: Provide sample request traces and redis-like dump by 2026-11-18
Maya: Stand up load-gen scenario and run repro with -long-context flag by 2026-11-20
Renee: Approve maintenance window for canary test on on-prem cluster by 2026-11-19
next_steps: Run repro harness for 48h with KV debug enabled
Exchange flame graphs and heap snapshots
Enable sticky routing for hot prefixes in canary
transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-11-12
- Start: 15:00 UTC
- Duration: ~58 minutes
- Attendees: Taylor (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Omar (Redwood CSM); Jordan (Lyra Platform), Renee (Lyra ML Infra), Samir (Lyra CTO), Priya (Lyra SRE)

Summary / Context (auto):
Customer running Redwood Private on-prem with VPC-like networking. Running multi-tenant inference for chatbots with long-context sessions (average 6-12k tokens, spikes to 30k). Recently seeing rising eviction rates and paging to local disk causing tail latency spikes. Want deep dive to find root cause and mitigations.

00:00:00 - Taylor (AE): All right folks, thanks for joining. quick agenda: reproduce the eviction pattern, review telemetry, propose mitigations, and define canary. Sound good?
00:00:15 - Jordan (Platform Eng): Yeah, that's perfect. we've been chasing this for a couple weeks now, um, tail latencies up and some OOM warnings... not full cluster crashes but chatter.
00:00:28 - Maya (SE): Can you describe the exact pattern you see? is it for a single model, or across variants?
00:00:35 - Priya (SRE): Mostly across two large models, the main customer-facing chat and an internal summarizer. The chat has the long contexts. The eviction rate climbs during sustained peak windows and then paging spikes.
00:00:50 - Renee (ML Infra): The KV hit rate drops from ~96% to 70% in about 20 minutes under load, but total memory usage looks stable, which is confusing.
00:01:05 - Maya (SE): OK that often points to prefix thrash — a lot of distinct prefixes being created or reused in slightly different ways. Are you doing per-user prefixes or per-session?
00:01:15 - Jordan: Per-session prefixes but with a conversation template we call 'customer-intake' that many sessions reuse. we think prefix reuse should help but maybe small differences create new prefixes.
00:01:30 - Taylor (AE): And this is on your on-prem Private deployment with our control plane in a peered VPC?
00:01:36 - Samir (CTO): Yes control plane peered. compute and KV store are inside our colo. we run SSD-backed local paging.
00:01:45 - Maya (SE): Got it. two immediate suspects: 1) prefix canonicalization mismatch, 2) aggressive KV eviction policy + prefetch heuristics not tuned for long context.
00:02:02 - Priya: we also did a rolling restart last week. after that the problem seemed worse for a few hours and then stabilized, but yesterday it flared again under traffic.
00:02:13 - Maya: Rolling restarts can cause re-warming issues; if your prefetch window is narrow, restarts will flush in-memory KV and prefetch isn't catching up.

00:05:00 - [Maya shares screen — telemetry graphs]
00:05:07 - Maya: here's the hit-rate dashboard. see the sudden decline here (pointing) coincident with page writes increasing. eviction spikes align with bursts. the paging latency distribution shifts to the right.
00:05:30 - Jordan: yep that's what we saw. also note the 'prefix-creation' metric — there's a big uptick at the same time.
00:05:42 - Taylor: Are you seeing a particular node or shard doing most of the paging?
00:05:47 - Priya: shard-3 tends to hit disk first. it's not always the same but shard-3 shows higher page-out counts.
00:05:57 - Maya: That suggests either uneven prefix hashing or one hot prefix mapped to that shard. can you share the prefix distribution histogram?
00:06:05 - Jordan: uploading now to the shared doc — link: <internal>/lyra/prefix-histogram-20261112.csv
00:06:18 - Maya: Hmm this shows a long tail: a small number of prefixes have extremely high cardinality while most are singletons. Classic hot-spot.
00:06:30 - Renee: The hot prefix corresponds to our intake template plus minor personalization tokens — so not identical but many similar keys.
00:06:40 - Maya: That is policy mismatch: small differences in the prefix string produce different keys. we should canonicalize or hash-normalize template variables before writing to KV.
00:06:50 - Jordan: We can do that but it's invasive across services. any runtime mitigations?
00:06:55 - Maya: A few: increase SLRU protected space for hot prefixes, enable sticky routing/affinity so those requests land on the shard with warmed KV, and bump prefetch depth for templates you mark as 'hot'.
00:07:10 - Taylor: Also consider short-circuiting long shared templates into a local in-memory L0 cache to avoid KV lookups for the first N tokens.

00:14:20 - Priya: quick question about paging: our on-prem nodes have NVMe for cache spill, but we see ~150ms 95th on page reads during burst. is that expected?
00:14:30 - Maya: 150ms is high; we'd expect NVMe to be lower unless you have IO contention or a synchronous write path. Are you using fsync on spill?
00:14:40 - Jordan: we left default fsync on for safety; maybe that's the culprit.
00:14:47 - Maya: If your throughput demands latency SLOs, consider async writeback with a short durability window, or move to an in-memory spill buffer with periodic checkpointing. also check kernel io_scheduler and cgroup IO limits.

00:20:05 - Renee: what about quantization and batching impact on KV behavior? we moved to int4 for cost and increased batch size for throughput. could that worsen eviction?
00:20:15 - Maya: quantization reduces memory for model weights but not KV. bigger batches increase parallel KV access which can magnify hot prefixes and lead to temporary memory pressure on a shard. batching also increases concurrent token generation and longer KV lifetimes per request.
00:20:30 - Taylor: so tradeoff — larger batches reduce per-token compute cost but amplify cache churn.
00:20:37 - Priya: any heuristic on batch size vs cache pressure?
00:20:41 - Maya: start by capping batch concurrency for long-context models and use dynamic batching that respects per-session affinity. also enable prefix coalescing in the runtime so duplicate prefix reads in a batch are de-duplicated.

00:25:50 - Jordan: we noticed that after rolling restart some nodes didn't re-prefetch the same prefixes and were essentially cold. is there a way to persist warmed prefixes across restarts?
00:25:59 - Maya: You can persist a compacted KV snapshot to shared storage and on restart quickly rehydrate hot prefixes. We offer a snapshot export tool. For on-prem you can use a shared NFS or object store. This reduces rewarm time.
00:26:14 - Jordan: We have S3-compatible object store. should work.

00:32:10 - Samir (CTO): Let's talk routing — is there a config we can tune so traffic for the intake template always routes to the same shard? we're worried about single-shard hotspots causing localized paging.
00:32:22 - Maya: Yes, enable sticky routing or use consistent hashing that includes a hot-prefix hint. For Private, we can set a route policy that pins certain prefix hashes to a subset of the cluster and reserve extra memory there.
00:32:38 - Taylor: This is similar to our 'pin-hot-prefix' feature; it creates a fast-path and increases prefetch and protected memory for pinned prefixes.
00:32:48 - Priya: how does that interact with autoscaling? if pinned shard fills up, will we get graceful fallback?
00:32:55 - Maya: we have fallback policy: route to a dedicated overflow pool or a lower-cost model variant. we can also enable automatic spillback to other shards with throttled request rates to avoid OOM.

00:38:00 - Renee: what's the recommended prefetch depth for long-contexts? we currently have it at 8 segments.
00:38:07 - Maya: for 6-12k contexts you may want 20-30 segments depending on tokenization density. but this increases memory; combine with hot-prefix pinning and L0 short-circuit to limit footprint.
00:38:22 - Jordan: any quick wins we can do without infra changes?
00:38:26 - Maya: canonicalize prefixes in the app layer, reduce batch concurrency for the problematic models, and temporarily increase prefetch for the top 5 prefixes. also disable blocking fsync on spill to reduce page latency.

00:45:10 - Taylor: operational checklist for canary: 1) pick small subset of users and flag intake template as pinned; 2) run load-gen for 24h with same request distribution; 3) capture perf counters and page traces; 4) iterate on prefetch depth and batch cap.
00:45:25 - Jordan: we'll need a maintenance window to change routing rules. that's fine.

00:50:05 - Priya: about telemetry — what queries should we run to detect prefix thrash early?
00:50:10 - Maya: watch new-prefix-rate, prefix-cardinality-per-minute, per-shard eviction-rate, page-reads/sec, prefetch-miss-rate, and tail kv read latencies. set anomaly alerts on prefix-cardinality delta > 200% in 5m window.
00:50:30 - Taylor: we'll send a sample Grafana dashboard and NRQL/PromQL queries.

00:54:40 - Action recap:
- Taylor: share diagnostic runbook + queries (by 2026-11-15)
- Jordan: upload traces and prefix histogram (by 2026-11-18)
- Maya: run load-gen and repro (by 2026-11-20)
- Renee: approve canary window (by 2026-11-19)

00:56:10 - Jordan: thanks everyone. one last question — for long-term, would Redwood recommend moving to Dedicated or keep Private on-prem?
00:56:20 - Taylor: If you want easier autoscaling and built-in snapshot storage and no fsync/IO fiddling, Dedicated simplifies ops, but Private gives you full data control. it's a cost/ops tradeoff.
00:56:32 - Samir: we'll evaluate; for now we need a short-term mitigation so customers don't see regressions.
00:56:40 - Maya: we'll follow up with the runbook and help set up the canary.
00:56:50 - Taylor: great — thanks all. we'll reconvene after the repro runs.
00:57:00 - Meeting ended
